extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer reviewers, and biomedical researchers involved in publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critique on the current biomedical peer review system, describing shortcomings and proposed reforms to improve reviewer selection, training, incentives, fraud prevention, and alternative models of review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and specialization of peer reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: The lack of formal training programs for peer reviewers places the scientific quality of biomedical publications at risk; training and specialization are needed, particularly for complex study types such as randomized controlled trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations include structured guidelines, courses for referees, formal annual education sessions on how to conduct peer review, and targeted training/specialization (e.g., for RCT review). The article cites an Appendix of uniform guidelines as useful for younger and less experienced reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer workload, timeliness and sustainability
rubrics_metrics.description: The exponential increase in manuscript submissions overburdens available qualified referees; the workload on individual reviewers appears to be reaching a 'breaking point' and threatens timeliness and quality of evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems should account for reviewer capacity, reduce unsustainable assignment volumes, and ensure timely completion. Metrics such as timely completion are candidates for incentive schemes (e.g., CME credits tied to timeliness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise and subject-matter matching
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal peer reviewer is an active scientist working in the same subspecialty 'niche' as the submitted paper to ensure appropriate technical scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should match reviewers to topic-specific expertise (publication record, expert lists). However, guidance recognizes trade-offs: ideal reviewers should not have current collaborations with authors, but may be competitors — a source of potential bias that must be managed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest identification and avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should have no current collaboration or professional liaison with submitting authors to avoid conflicts of interest; hidden conflicts (including competition for grants) may bias reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors are advised to investigate reviewer suitability by matching publication records and cross-checking for co-authorships with submitting authors. Processes to detect hidden conflicts should be implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to detect research misconduct, fraud, and redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers and editors must be able to recognize unethical research conduct, including fabricated data, plagiarism, redundant publications, and other misconduct that jeopardizes evidence-based medicine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend heightened scrutiny for signs of misconduct; consider additional specialist review (e.g., statisticians) and editorial workflows to investigate suspected fraud. Be aware that retractions likely represent only the 'tip of the iceberg.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of structured reporting standards and reviewer guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review has not evolved analogously to structured reporting standards (e.g., CONSORT for trials, QUOROM for meta-analyses); journals should provide uniform reviewer guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt and disseminate structured reviewer checklists/guidelines (the Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery provides an Appendix with reviewer guidelines). Such uniform guidance is especially helpful for less-experienced reviewers and can improve consistency across reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical review and methodological oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing skilled biostatistical review is important to ensure appropriate study design and valid analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some journals employ an MD/PhD biostatistician to review provisionally accepted manuscripts; routine statistical review for studies with complex analyses is recommended as part of quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives and recognition for high-quality reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals can incentivize and reward peer review work to improve quality and timeliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include providing continuing medical education (CME) credits for reviewers who meet defined criteria for timely and high-quality evaluations, and other formal recognition mechanisms that encourage sustained reviewer engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent reviewer selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer selection should be based on objective evidence of expertise, such as publication record and curated lists of topic experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery selects reviewers based on publication record and assigns from lists of experts. Editors should document and apply transparent selection methods to improve reviewer appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review quality metrics and a 'quality mark'
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective metrics can be used to quantify the quality and engagement of peer review (e.g., PRE score); a peer review 'quality mark' could be incorporated in publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested metrics include journal rejection rate (as a proxy), overall number of review cycles, number of referees assigned to a manuscript, commissioning of re-reviews, and application of editorial changes prior to acceptance. The PRE (peer review evaluation) score is cited as an example based on defined objective metrics including number of review cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative and supplemental peer review models
rubrics_metrics.description: Complementary peer review approaches may address shortcomings of the traditional model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives discussed include post-publication peer review, decoupled peer review, collaborative peer review, and portable peer review (including third-party evaluations paid by authors). Each model has distinct trade-offs and may supplement or replace parts of conventional peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention and detection of peer review fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review fraud (e.g., falsified contact information for suggested referees, peer review and citation rings) is a serious threat that can subvert review integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online submission/review systems need safeguards to verify reviewer identities and suggested contacts. The article cites a case of a peer review fraud ring leading to mass retractions, underscoring the need for editorial vigilance and technical checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility for streamlining and quality assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors have the ultimate duty to ensure a streamlined, fast-track, and high-quality peer review process; flaws in editorial handling will jeopardize evidence-based recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must spend time identifying suitable referees, verifying qualifications, avoiding conflicts of interest, and ensuring that commissioned reviews are comprehensive and returned within deadlines. Editorial policies should prioritize processes that protect publication quality over purely business or survival motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of commercial incentives and transparency about journal practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal business models (e.g., author-pays open-access) may create incentives that lower peer review thresholds; transparency about such effects is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track and, where possible, publish metrics such as rejection rates, review cycles, and editorial handling to help readers assess peer review rigour. Be cautious about treating acceptance in some open-access venues as equivalent to rigorous peer review when commercial incentives exist.
